content.text: Diffusion is the algorithm that is used by (most) modern AI systems to produce images. In this chapter we are going to explore a specific instance of that task: generate pictures of trees from the "tree photo distribution" and generating images of hand drawn eights from the "hand drawn eight distribution".
We are going to assume that we have access to a dataset with many photos of trees.
Here’s the full workflow for a diffusion model that we are going to cover:
Forward process:
Slowly add Gaussian noise to images until they turn into pure noise.
Reverse process:
Train a neural network to predict the mean for each pixel (
) in the previous time step and remove noise step-by-step.
Image generation:
Start with random noise and run the neural network in reverse
times to generate a realistic image.

This elegant approach combines simple Gaussian noise with the power of deep learning to generate stunning results! In parallel to generating trees, I will pull examples from a working diffusion model I built to create hand drawn number 8s. Here is an example of the end product. If I run the program 16 times, I would get 16 different hand drawn 8s.
Adding Noise

A great insight behind the diffusion algorithm is to take our dataset of images, and use it to create a dataset of images being generated from pure noise. To do this we supplement our dataset by iteratively adding gaussian noise to pixels, then train a deep learning model to remove noise.
A reasonable number of steps would be to add 10% noise each time step, so that after
timesteps each pixel is fully noise. Consider a single pixel.

This is where the machine learning comes in. How do we learn the reverse process in a principled way?
Learning the Reverse Process

It turns out it is sufficient to train a neural network which can predict the mean value of a pixel in a previous time step, based on the value of pixels in the current time step. Surprisingly, if we predict the mean, we can know the full sampling distribution!
Here is a picture of what our neural network could look like. It takes in an image at a given timestep, and for each pixel, it will predict the mean of the pixel before noise was added:
It can be trained on all the images generated in the "adding noise" step.

It was a big result from Physics that was discovered when folks were studying the random motion of particles in a fluid, that would cause the particles to disperse. Curious? The upshot of this result is that in order to reverse this process we only need to estimate the value
for each pixel in a previous timestep, given the pixels in a current timestep. Once we have the mean, we have the whole posterior distribution, and then we can sample from it!
The Neural Network for Reverse Sampling

Sampling an image is more work that predicting an image. But thanks to the critical fact, we can sample backwards as long as we know the mean of the distribution (we know its a normal and we know the variance). To that end we are going to build a neural network that can predict the mean of the distribution. Then we can denoise by sampling from the implied neural network.

There are many reasonable neural networks you could use to predict means (and that isn't the focus of this chapter). When we are predicting the mean of the pixel for the previous time step we use all the information we have: every pixel in time step
, which timestep we are on, and any information (eg text) that we have about what we are generating.
A common question is: if we can predict the mean of the pixels at time
, shouldn't we just use that as our sample at time
? The goal is to
sample
from the reverse process, not to estimate it's expectation. The reverse step is a whole Gaussian, not just its mean. Once the network gives us
we can reconstruct the Gaussian and sample. If you always just selected
as the previous pixel value you would generally get less faithful, less varied samples from the underlying distribution.
Training the Neural Network

We now have a machine learning challenge: learn to predict the value of a pixel before noise was added to it. How should we set up our “likelihood function” (equivalently, how could we set up a loss function)?
Because we want our model to be generative, instead of measuring how likely a single point is, the proper thing to do is to measure the quality of our predicted Gaussian. There are many good ways to
compare distributions
, but the easiest to optimize is KL divergence.

Happily in this case, because the distributions are Gaussian you can prove that minimizing the KL divergence is equivalent to minimizing the mean squared error of your predicted pixel and the actual pixel. See
Further Reading
for all the details.
At this point you have all the key concepts behind diffusion. Next steps could be to (1) implement it yourself or (2) to go deeper into the proofs of the critical facts we came across.
